summary: Correct layout and colours, but flat yellow slats on thin black lines read as a diagram, not moulded plastic and webbing.
critique: Length (~4.2 m, 9 rungs at ~0.45-0.5 m pitch) and rung width (~0.45 m) are right, and the slight waviness in the side straps is a good touch. Up close it is very simple. The rungs are flat rectangles of uniform saturated yellow with no thickness, curvature or moulded detail. Real rungs are 3-5 mm injection-moulded slats, often slightly convex or ribbed, with a visible buckle or slot clip at each end where the webbing threads through. Here the end 'clips' are just slightly wider pale squares. The side straps are black strips with no weave, no thickness and no edge highlight. They also don't drape: real 25 mm nylon webbing lies in loose S-curves, crosses over itself and twists, and lifts slightly where it threads through the rung clip. There are no end loops or handles, no carry bag and no tag. The material is a single matte yellow with no scuffs, grass stains or sun fading, so it looks brand new and CG.
suggestions: Model each rung as a 430 x 40 x 4 mm slat with a 2-3 mm convex camber and a 6 mm raised rim (about 40 tris), and give each end a 50 x 50 x 12 mm clip block with a slot that the strap visibly enters and exits (about 24 tris per clip). The ends should cast a small contact shadow.

Give the straps 25 mm width and 1.5 mm thickness as a two-sided ribbon. Add a 100-150 mm sewn loop at each end of both straps. Let straps cross the rung clips and sag 5-15 mm between rungs, with random per-segment yaw of up to 3 degrees.

Materials: rung yellow albedo about (0.80, 0.62, 0.05) at roughness 0.55, with a faint moulding sheen. Webbing: black albedo 0.04, roughness 0.8, plus a tiling 2-channel weave normal map (64 px is enough).
Wear: a grass-stain/dirt mask on the underside 30% of rungs and the strap ends, and scuffed lighter edges on the rung rims. A 128 px shared atlas covers the whole asset.
Optionally add a variant with one strap twisted or a rung slid off-centre so instanced ladders don't all look factory-laid.
renderer_notes: Grass blades occlude the flat strap at grazing angles in the side view; that is the lawn, not the asset.

summary: Convincing anti-vandal welfare cabin with steps, shutters and services, let down by a container-style roof, spray-pattern rust and boxy shutter housings.
critique: Proportions are right for a 32 x 10 ft unit (about 9.75 x 3.05 x 2.44 m). The corrugated walls, dark corner posts and rails, timber/concrete pad footings, galvanised step unit with handrails, door with signage, roller-shutter window boxes, electrical hook-up box and trailing cables are the right vocabulary, and from the three-quarter view it reads as a real site cabin. Problems: (1) The roof is container-style shallow corrugation running the full width. Real anti-vandal cabins have a flat or slightly cambered steel roof with a raised perimeter upstand, corner lifting eyes and often a drip edge. The ponding stains are a good idea, but they look like big soft decals. (2) Rust is uniform random dots and splatters spread evenly across the walls. Real cabin rust starts at the bottom rail, corner posts, around window frames, at forklift pockets and in streaks running down from fixings. (3) The roller-shutter boxes are plain bevelled rectangles with no end caps, guide rails or bottom bar, and the shutter slats are faint. (4) There are no forklift pockets in the base rail, no lifting eyes, no vents (each cabin has wall vents and a WC extract) and no gutter or downpipe. (5) The off-white walls read too clean and too uniform. They need grime on the lower third and dirt washing down from the roof edge. (6) The end-wall window is a flat inset with no frame depth.
suggestions: Replace the corrugated roof with a flat sheet 2-3 degrees off level, with a 60 mm perimeter upstand and four corner lifting eyes (about 200 tris). Keep the ponding stains, but break them into 2-3 tide-mark rings.

Add forklift pockets to the long base rail: two 300 x 100 mm recessed openings per side, 2 m apart. Add 2-3 louvred vent grilles (200 x 200 mm, normal-mapped) high on the walls, and a 75 mm downpipe at one corner.

Drive rust and grime with a vertex-colour or world-space mask: heavy on the bottom 300 mm rail, the corner posts and around window frames, with vertical streaks running down from roof-edge fixings. Remove the evenly spread dots. Use one 512 px tiling grime atlas shared across all cabins.

Shutter boxes: add end caps, 30 mm side guide channels down the window reveal, a bottom bar with a padlock hasp, and a slat normal map at about 75 mm pitch. Recess the windows 80 mm with a visible frame.
Tint the walls off-white to about (0.72, 0.72, 0.68) with roughness 0.6 and slight per-panel albedo variation (plus or minus 3%) so the corrugation doesn't read as one sheet.
renderer_notes: No GI means the shadowed underside and steps read slightly too dark; that is acceptable.

summary: Good front-tip dumper silhouette, with fold-down ROPS, beacon, lights, a plated rear and chunky tyres, but it lacks an articulation joint and real grime, and the skip is undersized for a 6 t class.
critique: Strong points: the side profile (skip over the front axle, operator seat behind it, rear engine pod with the ROPS hoop) is correct for a front-tip site dumper. The tyres have a real lug tread, the wheels have hub and bolt detail, and the ROPS has fold hinges, work lights and an amber beacon. The SWL decal, chevrons, number plate and lights on the rear are good. Problems: (1) There is no articulation joint. A real Thwaites/JCB 6 t dumper is articulated in the middle with a large pivot and steering rams, but here the chassis between the axles is a plain yellow box beam. (2) The skip looks small and narrow for 6 t. A real 6 t skip is about 3.2-3.5 m3 and spans the full machine width (about 2.2-2.35 m), overhanging the front wheels. Here it sits within the track width and the wheels poke out beyond it. The skip should also have a reinforced front lip and rolled top edge, and the tip rams should be visible. (3) The front has a strange exposed horizontal bar and bracket, like a tow bar, under the skip, and the front bumper box is plain. (4) The paint is near-uniform clean yellow with only faint grime. Site dumpers are coated in mud: wheel arches, tyres, skip interior and lower chassis. (5) The engine cover is a smooth rounded box with no grilles on its sides or top, no exhaust stack shape detail and no hand holds. (6) The steering wheel and controls float in an open void without a floor plate or step, and there is no seat belt.
suggestions: Add a centre articulation joint. Split the chassis at about 45% of the wheelbase, with an 18-20 cm diameter pivot pin housing top and bottom and two steering rams (100 mm cylinders) either side (about 400 tris).

Widen the skip to about 2.25 m at the rim so it overhangs the front tyres by 80-100 mm each side. Deepen it to about 1.1 m, add a 60 mm rolled top lip, three vertical stiffener ribs per side, and the two tip rams visible beneath the front.

Grime pass: a world-space height mask for mud on the bottom 600 mm, the tyres and the arches. Put dried concrete splash (albedo about 0.55 grey, roughness 0.9) on the skip lip and interior. Add a chipped-paint edge mask on the skip rim and ROPS. Use one shared 1k grime atlas.

Give the engine pod louvred side grilles (normal-mapped panels about 400 x 250 mm), an exhaust stack with a rain cap, and a step plate with anti-slip tread on each side. Close the operator floor with a checker-plate footwell.
Remove or justify the exposed front cross-bar. If it is the skip pivot, show it as two pivot bosses on the chassis front with pins, not a free-floating rod.
renderer_notes: Shadows and lighting are fine; the long ROPS shadow is correct for a low sun.

summary: Correct flat-top crane layout with lattice mast, jib, counter-jib ballast, cab and trolley, but the lattice is thin and simplified and the base and reeving are underdetailed.
critique: Good: the overall flat-top proportions (jib about 60 m, counter-jib with stacked concrete ballast blocks, machinery and an electrics cabinet), the cab at the slewing head, the trolley with a hook block, the mast with rest platforms and bolted section joints (grey plates every few metres), and the Heras-fenced concrete base all read correctly at distance. Problems: (1) The mast lattice is a single diagonal per face plus horizontals, all drawn as thin flat bars. A real mast (about 1.6 x 1.6 m) uses tubular or angle chords about 150-200 mm, with K or zig-zag bracing and visibly thicker chords than braces. Here the chords and braces look the same thickness, which makes it look like a model kit. (2) There is no internal ladder with a hoop cage. The rest platforms are there, but the ladder that links them is not visible. (3) The hoist rope is a single line. A real crane runs 2 or 4 falls with a pulley block on the trolley and a load block with the hook, so you see 2-4 parallel ropes. (4) The slewing unit is a box. It needs a visible slewing ring, a turntable platform with handrails, and the transition piece. (5) The base is a white slab on grass. Real bases are an excavated, cast pad with foundation anchors and a cross-base or fixing angles, mud, a cable drum and a site electrics box. (6) The colour is uniform saturated yellow with no dirt, galvanised bolts or faded paint, and there is no brand or load-chart signage on the jib (load-rating boards are normally hung on the jib).
suggestions: Rebuild mast sections as 4 square chords (about 160 mm) with Z-bracing of 80 mm tubes, so the chord-to-brace thickness ratio is about 2:1. Use one 5.6 m section mesh instanced up the mast (about 600 tris per section) and add an inner ladder with a safety cage down one face.
Show the reeving: two ropes from the trolley sheaves down to a separate yellow-and-black hook block (about 0.6 x 0.4 x 0.8 m) with a ball weight. This is an instanced line pair, so it is cheap.
Model the slewing assembly: ring (2 m diameter, 0.3 m deep), a turntable platform with toe boards and handrails, and a 2.5 m cab with glazing on 3 sides and a roof wiper.
Base: sink the pad 100 mm into a dirt-coloured ground decal, show 4 corner anchor plates, and add a site electrics cabinet and a cable running to the fence.
Add 3-4 load-rating boards along the jib (1.5 x 1 m, white with black numerals). Add mild paint fade and a dirt-gradient mask on the lower mast (vertex colour, no extra textures).
renderer_notes: Thin members alias at distance; enable MSAA or alpha-to-coverage on the lattice. The shadow-map resolution also loses mast detail in the cast shadows.

summary: Credible rebounder: tubular frame, A-frame leg, orange bungee lacing and a white net, but the net reads as slack wobbly lines rather than a tensioned elastic mesh.
critique: Proportions (about 1.2 x 1.2 m frame, rear prop leg with angle-adjust knobs, rubber feet) are right, and the orange shock-cord lacing round the frame is the detail that sells it. The frame has a reasonable powder-coat grunge. Problems: (1) The net cords wobble randomly as if slack, but a rebounder net is drum-tight. Lines should be straight, with slight pincushion pull toward each bungee anchor. In the side view the top edge of the net has odd curls and kinks. (2) The net is single flat white lines with no cord thickness or knots at intersections, and no braid or shading. (3) The net border rope and bungee anchors are good, but the bungees are evenly spaced simple 'V' shapes without a hook at the frame. Real ones loop around the tube. (4) The rear leg is a single thin U-tube and the hinge knobs are basic cylinders. Real units have a clamp bracket with a T-handle or star knob and a ratchet plate. (5) There is no ground-peg or stake detail, and no brand label or sticker on the frame.
suggestions: Tension the net: drive cord intersections from a straight grid with a small pull (10-20 mm) toward the nearest bungee anchor, and remove random wobble. Keep the mesh at about 100 mm squares. Render as camera-facing ribbons about 5 mm wide, or a 2-sided alpha-tested card with a 256 px net texture that has knot bumps (much cheaper than geometry).
Bungees: model each as a closed loop wrapping the frame tube (8-sided, 6 mm), so the cord visibly goes around the tube (about 30 tris each).
Replace hinge knobs with a 60 mm star knob plus a clamp plate and a ratchet disc. Add rubber end-caps to all tube ends.
Add a small sticker or label on the frame top rail and scuffing on the bottom rail and feet, where it is dragged across grass.
Give the net a slight off-white (0.85) with dirt darkening on the lower third and the ball-impact centre.
renderer_notes: The net cords are too thin for the shadow map, so the net casts no shadow. That is a renderer limitation and not counted against the asset.

summary: Correct modern LED sports floodlight layout (lens array, visor, trunnion yoke, finned rear, driver box), but it looks like clean grey boxes with flat-texture optics.
critique: The architecture is right: a rectangular die-cast body, a glass front with a grid of TIR lens optics and visible LED dies, a top visor, side trunnions with an aiming scale, a U-yoke, finned heat sink on the back and a driver/gear box with a label and cable gland. Where it falls down: (1) Everything is flat grey (about 0.5 albedo) with almost no bevels, so it reads as CAD boxes. A real fixture (e.g. ArenaVision or Musco TLC) has heavily radiused die-cast edges, chamfered fins and cast ribs. (2) The lenses are a flat texture behind a flat glass plate. There is no glass reflection layer, no lens depth or parallax, and the module seams look printed on. (3) The visor is a thin flat plate with no side cheeks or louvres, and it looks pasted on. (4) The yoke is a thin strap. Real yokes are thick steel (about 10-12 mm) with a mounting plate, bolts and a large aiming-angle indicator. The side view shows the yoke and body as a slab without depth breakup. (5) There is no weathering: no dirt streaks from the visor, no bird mess, no oxidised fasteners, no safety-wire lanyard.
suggestions: Bevel all body and visor edges with a 6-10 mm radius (2-segment), and round the heat-sink fin tips. This adds about 1k tris but removes the CAD look.

Optics: add a separate front glass quad with a clear-coat (roughness 0.05, F0 0.04) so it picks up sky reflections, and recess the lens array 15 mm. Use a 256 px lens normal map with a concentric TIR profile plus parallax, and an emissive mask on the dies for night use.
Visor: give it 30 mm side cheeks and a folded front lip, and optionally internal glare-control louvres (3 slats).
Thicken the yoke to 12 mm, add a 200 x 200 mm mounting plate with 4 bolts, a protractor aiming scale on the trunnion, and a stainless safety cable.
Weathering: dark streaks down the glass from the visor edge, dust on the top fins, and slight colour variation between powder-coat grey (0.38-0.42) and anodised trim.
renderer_notes: No SSR or environment reflections makes the glass front look flatter than it would in a game engine with reflection probes.

summary: Convincing galvanised 1100 L Eurobin with green plastic lid, side trunnions, swaged bands, braked castors and decals. It is close to good, but too clean and the lid lacks moulded detail.
critique: Proportions (about 1.37 x 1.26 x 1.0 m), the tapered body with pressed horizontal swage bands, the comb-lift trunnions, the braked castors with red pedals, the 'B12' stencil and the council stickers are all right. It reads as a real Eurobin from every angle. Remaining gaps: (1) The galvanised steel is a uniform mid grey with mild variation. Real galvanising shows a spangle or crystalline pattern, white-rust bloom, dark grime at the bottom and around the lid seam, and dents. (2) The lid is a smooth, slightly soft green slab with a raised panel. Real HDPE lids have moulded strengthening ribs, an embossed logo or recycling symbol, a moulded hinge knuckle at the back and a distinct front lip. (3) The lid handles look like bent rod rather than moulded plastic grips. (4) The swage bands look like added rings rather than pressed into the sheet. They need a matching shallow inward groove on either side. (5) There is no drain plug detail at the bottom front, no lock, and no grime or leachate staining down from the lid.
suggestions: Add a galvanised material: albedo 0.55-0.62 with a 512 px tiling spangle normal/roughness map (roughness 0.35-0.6 variation), white-rust patches, and a dirt gradient on the bottom 300 mm and under the lid rim via vertex colour.

Lid: add 4-6 shallow moulded ribs on the top, an embossed recycling or council logo (normal map), a hinge knuckle (3 barrels) across the back edge, and moulded recessed hand-grips at the front instead of the rod handles.
Make the swage bands pressed: model each as an outward bead with an inward groove above and below. That is 2 extra edge loops per band, under 100 tris.
Add 2-3 shallow dent normal decals per instance (randomised), a drain bung at the front base, and brown leachate streaks running down from the lid seam.
renderer_notes: The lid looks slightly washed and over-bright in the close-up; part of that is sky ambient without GI.

summary: Believable construction-site hoarding board with good graphics, but text glyph glitches, a dark CG back panel and unrefined timber posts and struts hold it back.
critique: Good: the size and layout, the red/white/green UK site-board graphic with contractor details, PPE pictograms and safety banner, the aluminium edge trim, the two posts with raking struts and the disturbed earth at post bases. Problems: (1) Text artefacts: 'SAFETY' renders with a stray accent dot over the S, and 'ACT' has a stray mark over the T. This is an obvious glyph or kerning bug that any player reading the board will see. (2) The back of the board is a near-black slate panel with a smudgy texture. A real site board is printed Dibond (white or silver back) or painted plywood (raw ply or white). Dark grey reads as an untextured placeholder. (3) The posts are pale beige with an even grain and very clean square tops. Real ones are tanalised green/brown softwood (100 x 100 mm), with checks and splits, a darker wet band at the ground and coach bolts through the board battens. (4) The struts end in the ground with no stake or base plate, and one has a kinked foot. The back battens have no fixings. (5) The printed face is too clean: no dirt splash on the lower 200 mm, no UV fade on the red, no cable-tie holes or screw caps.
suggestions: Fix the text renderer so stray diacritics don't appear on 'S' and 'T' (likely a glyph-atlas offset or wrong code point). Bake the board face to a 1024 x 512 texture once so instancing costs nothing.
Back face: use a white or silver Dibond back (albedo about 0.75, roughness 0.4) with the battens screwed on. Show 4-6 coach-bolt heads per batten and the M10 bolts through the posts.

Posts: tanalised-timber albedo about (0.42, 0.38, 0.28), with a darker 300 mm wet band at the ground, end-grain checks on the post tops and 1-2 shallow split normals. Make struts 75 x 50 mm and end each in a 400 mm pointed stake beside a small earth scar.
Weather the face: mud splash on the bottom 150 mm, 5-10% fade on the red band, slight wave or bow in the panel. Add 4 dome-head screw caps at the corners.
renderer_notes: None. The board is lit and shadowed correctly.

summary: Brick barrel-vault halls and outbuildings give a plausible site, but they are blocky and lightly detailed, and the 'main building' view shows a container compound instead.
critique: From the aerial view there are three red-brick barrel-roofed halls, a flat-roofed block, two small pitched sheds and a pavilion or shelter. Up close (pitch view), the hall is a brick box with a curved gable in brick, a pale curved roof with a dark rooflight, and a single continuous strip of dark clerestory glazing. Problems: (1) The brick texture is blotchy and low-frequency at mid range, with no visible coursing or mortar, so the gable reads as a red noise pattern. A curved brick gable on a barrel-vault hall is also unusual. These are normally clad steel or have a brick plinth with metal cladding above. (2) There are no doors, roller shutters, entrance canopy, signage, downpipes, gutters, external lights or plant, so the building has no human scale. (3) The roof has no seams, ribs or eaves detail. (4) The small pitched sheds are plain boxes with dark gable faces. (5) The view labelled as the main building shows only two green ISO containers in a fenced gravel compound, plus a ride-on mower and a low-poly faceted beige boulder or heap at the edge. The boulder is clearly lower quality than everything else. The containers themselves are decent: corrugation, rust at corners, 'KESTREL' stencil. (6) Sunday-league grounds typically have a modest single-storey brick or clad pavilion with changing rooms, a veranda and a car-park frontage. That hero building isn't shown or doesn't read.
suggestions: Make a hero clubhouse or pavilion the focus: a single-storey brick plinth (about 1 m) with profiled metal or timber cladding above, a pitched roof, a veranda facing the pitch, glazed double doors, changing-room doors with signage, gutters and downpipes, external bulkhead lights and a club-crest sign. Use a modular kit of about 3k tris per 6 m bay.

Halls: replace the brick gable with profiled steel cladding (normal-mapped trapezoidal profile at 333 mm pitch) over a 2 m brick plinth with a soldier course. Add a 4 x 4 m roller shutter, a personnel door, gutters, downpipes, standing-seam ribs on the roof and rooflight panels in a regular pattern.

Brick: use a 512 px tileable brick texture at true scale (215 x 65 mm brick, 10 mm mortar), with mortar normal and roughness and per-brick colour variation, plus a mid-distance macro variation so the gable doesn't read as noise.
Replace the faceted beige boulder or heap with a smoothed spoil or sand heap (a displaced dome with a soil texture), or remove it.
Point the 'main building' review camera at the actual clubhouse, so it can be judged.
renderer_notes: Aerial haze and distance flatten the buildings; the brick blotchiness, though, is texture scale, not the renderer.

summary: Varied, realistic car models in rows, but the car park itself is an unmarked, unworn pale slab with no bays, kerbs or drainage.
critique: The cars are the strongest part: varied makes, body styles and colours, number plates, decent wheels and glazing, and believable scale against the bollards. The parking surface lets it down badly. (1) There are no white bay lines, no disabled or parent bays, no arrows, and no hatched areas. Cars are lined up only by convention, so the layout looks unplanned and some cars sit at odd spacings. (2) The surface is a uniform pale concrete grey. A UK sports-club car park is usually dark asphalt (albedo about 0.08-0.12) or tarmac with lighter wheel-track wear, oil stains, patched repairs, gullies and manhole covers, or a loose gravel car park with potholes. (3) There are no kerbs or edging between the car park and the grass. The asphalt simply meets the lawn. (4) There are no lamp columns, signage (pay/display or 'club members only'), a barrier, or trolleys and bins. The bollards along the edge help. (5) The cars all sit perfectly level with identical clean paint, with no dirt and no rain spots. (6) In the aerial view the car park is a rectangle of pale tone with dense cars; a real one would follow the entrance road layout.
suggestions: Paint 2.4 x 4.8 m bays with 100 mm white lines (a decal strip mesh or a single tiling line texture with UV offset), plus 1-2 disabled bays with a blue symbol, direction arrows on the aisle and a hatched no-parking area by the entrance.

Change the surface to dark asphalt: albedo 0.09-0.12, roughness 0.85, with a 1k tiling aggregate normal map. Add a macro layer of lighter tyre-wear tracks along the aisles, dark oil drips under the bay centres, 2-3 patch repairs and a drainage gully every 20 m.
Add 125 mm precast concrete kerbs at the edges (one instanced 915 mm mesh, about 40 tris) and a dropped kerb at the entrance.
Add 2-4 8 m lamp columns, a club entrance sign and a height barrier, all from the existing kit.
Vary car instances with a per-instance dirt amount (0-0.4 on the lower body and wheels) and slight suspension height or roll offsets, to remove the showroom uniformity.
renderer_notes: Uniform sky ambient makes the slab look even paler. Real asphalt would still read dark.

summary: Pitch markings, goals, mannequin walls, poles, cones and balls are all present and plausibly placed, but the grass surface is flat and the multi-grid markings read busy and undersized.
critique: Good: white line markings with a centre circle, a worn centre spot and goalmouth wear patches (visible in the aerial view), goals with nets, a yellow free-kick mannequin wall, slalom poles, cones, scattered balls and portable goals at the far end. It feels like a real training session area. Problems: (1) The grass is a flat, uniform green with a faint smudge for the wear. There is no mowing stripe pattern (most clubs stripe even training pitches), no clumping or colour variation, and no rough edges between pitches. (2) Multiple overlapping grids and dashed lines in the distance read as noise. Real training grounds use separate grids with distinct marking colours (white plus yellow or blue for small-sided), not a tangle. (3) The ball and cone instances are tiny specks with no shadow, so they look sprinkled on. (4) There are no spectator rails, dugouts or team shelters, storage boxes or ball-stop netting behind goals. For a Sunday-league ground, ball-stop netting and a rail around the main pitch are expected. (5) The line width and paint look clean and uniform, without the soft, slightly broken edges of painted grass lines.
suggestions: Add mowing stripes as alternating light and dark bands (5-6 m wide) in the pitch shader, using a world-space direction parameter per pitch. Add a low-frequency colour and roughness noise, and stronger, browner wear on the goalmouths and centre circle.
Mark small-sided grids in a second colour (yellow or blue) and reduce overlapping lines. Draw lines 100-120 mm wide with a noise-broken edge alpha.

Add a 1.1 m spectator rail around the main pitch (instanced 2.5 m post-and-rail segments), two 6 m team shelters and ball-stop netting (5 m high, 30 m long) behind each goal. These are cheap tiled alpha nets on posts.
Ensure balls and cones cast contact shadows (a blob-shadow decal is enough), and cluster them realistically: in bags or carts, along cone lines, by the goals.
Add mud or worn bare patches near gate entries and dugouts.
renderer_notes: Small props lose shadow-map shadows at this distance; blob shadows would fix that cheaply.

summary: A sensible site plan in a patchwork-field setting with hedgerow trees, but the distant fields are flat tiles, hedges are thin lines and the near trees and hedges are only fair.
critique: Layout logic is good: an access road from the lane, the car park near the entrance, buildings clustered centrally, pitches arranged in a grid, maintenance compounds at the periphery, and boundary hedges with trees. The near oaks and birches in the ground-level views have good silhouettes. Problems: (1) Distant farmland is flat-coloured rectangles (yellow, brown, green) with hard edges and no crop rows, tramlines or texture. It reads as a game map, not countryside. (2) Field hedges are 1-pixel dark lines in the aerial view with evenly spaced lollipop trees. Real UK hedgerows are 1.5-2.5 m tall and 1-2 m wide, with irregular gaps, gates and field-corner trees. (3) The site ground is one uniform mown-lawn colour everywhere, including around buildings and on verges, with no rough grass, paths, wear lines or ditches. (4) Roads are flat grey strips with no verges, kerbs, white lines or passing places. (5) The tree distribution is too even, with similar spacing and sizes across the whole site. (6) The near hedge in the ground views is a long, straight, uniform green box.
suggestions: Give distant fields tiling crop textures (wheat rows, ploughed furrows, pasture) with tramline decals and soft field-edge margins (a 3-5 m grass headland). A shared 512 px atlas of 4 crop types will do.

Build hedgerows as instanced irregular hedge chunks (about 5 m modules, 1.8-2.5 m tall, 1.2-1.8 m wide, varied heights) with 10-15% random gaps and a 5-bar field gate at each field entrance. Place standard trees at irregular 20-60 m intervals, preferring corners.

Add ground variety: longer rough grass (darker, yellower) outside the mown pitch areas, worn desire-line paths from the car park to the pitches, gravel paths around buildings, and a drainage ditch along the boundary.
Roads: a 5.5 m single-track lane with grass verges, a broken centre line only on the main road, and a bell-mouth junction at the entrance.
Cluster trees in copses and along boundaries with size variation (plus or minus 30% scale), instead of a uniform scatter.
renderer_notes: Aerial haze and no GI flatten the macro landscape; that is acceptable for the renderer, but the field tiles' lack of texture is the asset.
